NATIONAL ENDOWMENT FOR THE ARTS
INSTITUTE OF JAZZ STUDIES

Interview of
ANDREW BLAKENEY
Conducted by Vi Redd

S. & S. REPORTING CO., INC.
Court Reporters—Notaries
132 Nassau Street
New York City
2915
WOrth 2 2943
Good afternoon, Mr. Andy Blakeney.

I am Andrew Blakeney, birth dated June 10, 1898, born Quitman, Mississippi. I am the son of Thomas and Anna Lucie Price Blakeney. I am the grandson of Lucie Price and Madison Price. I don't recall my paternal grandparents.

My grandmother was brought to Mississippi from Virginia by some people as a slave in her teens. Years later, she was permitted to marry the house slave by the name of Luke. Twelve children resulted from that union. My mother, Anna Lucie, was the eleventh child. My mother--the two youngest--were sent to Meridian to school by the big city just fifteen miles north of Enterprise.
One year later she went to Quitman, the county seat of Clark County to receive a license to teach. There

she met my father who was already a teacher They were married in June, 1897. I was born June 10, 1898 on a farm my father bought before he married my mother. Eight more children followed me. That ended my mother's teaching career.

My father was born in Quitman, Mississippi, November 29, 1864. The year before the surrender he always told it. He was the youngest of seven. At four years old his mother passed, not knowing who or what his father was; a white family took him in in their home.

The wife, a Mistress Bailey, taught him to read and write. At the age of twelve or thirteen he had to leave the white family and he started living with his older brothers and their children, who were about his same age.
He continued to study and had plenty of books. After he was grown and out on his own, his first job naturally was

teaching school.
I first attended school September, 1903. My papa took me to that one room school on the back of a mule and delivered me to Professor McGowan. I breezed through all grades up to the seventh, kind of lonely because I was the only big boy in school. All the other families kept their boys home to help on the farm.
Papa wouldn't let me go to Meridian so I could finish school, so I quit that eighth grade school where I knew almost as much as the teachers.

I went to work at a sawmill.
I was still unhappy. Just before my sixteenth birthday, I ran away from home.

I didn't stay long the first time. After a couple more runaways I was in Chicago, the year 1917. Young, independent and determined to make it on my own I had the usual menial jobs, dishwasher, porter, messenger boy, finally ending up in
the stockyards in a skilled job; musical career.
Back home in school Dad taught me how to read vocal music. I took also piano lessons; dropped piano after leaving home.

1919 in Chicago I decided I was going to take up music and I decided that the instrument would be trumpet. I made arrangements with W.L. Jackson Music School which was the most popular school on the south side of Chicago in those days. I stayed with him three years; this is 1922 now.

After that I organized my own amateur band, started playing for small parties; rented a hall, promoted weekend dances, catering to high school kids. It was rough but I survived. All through this I was working every day in the stock-yard.
1924. One Sunday night after making the rounds of the music joints, I

stopped by an after hours joint close to my home. I asked the leader where was the trumpet player and he said home sick. I said I play a little trumpet and I don't live far. He said go get it and come sit in. So I sat in and played until 6:00 A.M. closing time and the leader said, "The boss likes your playing, you can have this job if you want to. So twelve midnight to six, seven nights a week; you will have to join the union."
I just had time to change clothes and go to the stockyard. That one week I did a double shift and after that I said goodby stockyard. That was October, 1924. I haven't been to a stockyard since.
I stayed on this job seven months. By then I was exposed to most of the big shot leaders such as Joe Oliver--
Mr. Blakeney, was that the King Oliver?
That was the
King Oliver. Charlie Cook, Dave Peyton and others.
Erskine Tate was a leader of the famous Vendome Orchestra and he was the stepson of my music teacher, W. L. Jackson.
Mr. Blakeney, was that your first music teacher?
Yes it was--no, not my first, because I told you I took piano lessons in Mississippi.
I see.
My aunt gave me piano lessons in Mississippi.
Maybe you'd like to tell us just a little bit about him.
W.L. Jackson was a great talker. He used to claim to be one of the best violinists in the country, and after I had my lesson every night he would sit down and just talk about his experiences.
He would talk about how he
raised Erskine and his brother Charles. His brother Charles played trumpet, and Erskine played violin, and how he used to take him to recitals and how good they were and he would brag about them.

When they moved to Chicago, he separated from their mother. He wasn't the father of these kids, he was just the step-father; he married their mother. She had her own music school and he had his own music school.

W.L. Jackson, I kind of liked him because I liked the way he talked;and then after I was with him three years, he said I think you're good enough now, you ought to go down to the union and kind of work yourself in with the professionals. Of course instead of doing that I did it differently, I went with the band and started out that way.
The last job I had in Chicago was with my own band of eleven pieces. The Old Lincoln Gardens where Joe Oliver was playing burned down early in the year. It
was closed. They combined from the west side both the places; remodeled it and renamed it the Charleston Cafe.

It was there in mid October when I took my band after playing for several weeks. I suddenly told Shirley Clay, my second trumpet player, that I was quitting and going to California and I wanted him to take over the band. This is November, 1925.
What happened that you suddenly decided to come to California at that time, Mr. Blakeney?
Domestic problems.
I see.

I arrived in Los Angeles on Thanksgiving Day, 1925 to play great with the Sunnyland Band. For certain reasons I did not play with that band, so my first job was with Johnny Mitchell and the cafe downtown L.A., called the Italian Village.
Johnny was the leader on sax, Kenny Prince on piano, Les Hite, sax, Lionel Hampton, drums, myself on trumpet and a banjo player, I don't remember his name.
I stayed with Johnny until May, 1926. I played with Kencan Henry, Frank, Little Cotton Club, jobs, casuals, in Los Angeles and San Francisco.
October 1926 back with Johnny Mitchell.
Mr. Blakeney, was this about the time that you did your first recording with the Sonny--with Clay's group?
Yes it was about that time.

Sonny Clay came up to me and said that he was going to make some records and he wanted to know if I would mind playing on it. I told him yes, and so he was going to record two numbers, one on each side and he wanted me to play the hot cords
along with the rest of the band, the band was going to back me up. He regular trumpet player, Ernie Coycault was just a straight man, he didn't play hot jazz, and he wanted me to play the hot chords.
Also, Sonny wanted me to rehearse with him because he was expecting to enlarge his band and if he added another trumpet he was going to put me on, but that did never come around.

October 1926 I rejoined Johnny Mitchell who had an offer to go to Honolulu. I had just got back from San Franciso, I think it was about Thursday and he called me at my house--I called him to let him know I was in town, and I said I'm sleeping now because I drove all night from San Francisco, call me back this afternoon. And so he did. This was Thursday and he said they had a job to go to San Francisco--Honolulu--Saturday. I said what? He said yes, it's all made up with the tip and the
money, the contract is all signed. I said I have to think this over, give me another day to think a little bit. I just got here and my wife don't want me to leave right away again.
Anyway, I decided to go. In the band was myself, Gene Wright on piano, Lee Gibson on drums, C. L. Burke and myself on trumpet. Johnny had a contract, three months, with a three-month option.
We held the option, not the boss. If we wanted to work for another three months, we could; if we didn't we were free to come back home.
Also, any one man in the band could veto, and I was the veto. I didn't want to stay another three months so the whole band had to leave.
That was very interesting; that was some kind of contract, wasn't it, Mr. Blakeney?
It was written
in the contract that everybody had to agree to stay. If one man didn't want to stay, everybody had to leave.
On January 1, 1927 we caught the boat and came back to L.A.

That was a very interesting job; I can remember Gene Wright, he was one of the better piano players in Los Angeles at that time, but he wasn't very popular. He liked to play classics, he liked to run liked a man who all over the piano. But we/played rhythm, you know, backed us up on our horns, and we talked to him so much he'd get mad and then he'd play rhythm. Poor fellow is gone now; in fact, everybody in that band is gone now. Gene's gone, Fields gone, Lee's gone. Nobody left but me.
What was Honolulu like in those days?
Well, it was nothing like it is today. In fact, there were no colored people over there. We
were all young and healthy. One of the reasons I didn't want to stay over there was because I wanted my wife with me.
It was predominantly Oriental people there?
Mostly Orientals; Hawaiians.
And Polynesians. I guess it was very seldom that they saw colored musicians.
It was.
As we were called at that time. What was the reception? How did they receive you?
Very good. They liked our music. Except Johnny didn't like the posters they had out on us. It said five musicians--five black musicians, and they're all black. He made them tear the posters down.
What year was that?
Well at that time there were some very mixed feelings about the connotation "black", which is quite different than it is today.

That's about all I can remember about it except that in the latter part of our trip, the boss sent us on a tour of the other islands, playing theaters. We went to Maui, and the big island Honolulu, I mean the Hawaiian Island called Hilo *(the correct spelling) and we just broke it up on the stage. That Gene Wright, he could play all over the piano.
That must have been some experience for you.
Oh, yes. I enjoyed it except I was lonesome over there by myself. No wife, no girlfriend, no nothing.
That's all I can say about Honolulu right now.
*Hilo is the major city on the island named Hawaii.
Back in L.A., still with Johnny Mitchell's band, we started playing theaters, clubs, dance halls, up and down the coast, including movies; the silent pictures, I'm talking about.
Mr. Blakeney, tell us a little bit about the movies and the conditions at that time for black musicians, mainly in the silent movies at that time.
We did quite a bit of work in silent movies, and one of the social hour jobs out there was Satchel McVea. (spelling).
Indeed a legend, Mr. Satchel McVea.

I was on one job out there with him, the name of the picture was Breakfast at Sunrise, at Universal, and the star was Constance Talmadge. In those days musicians would actually play to entertain the stars while they were acting.
That was during the
Yes. It was supposed to give them inspiration. If they wanted a sweet waltz we'd play that; if they wanted something hot we'd play that.
That was all atmospheric?
That's what it was, atmospheric.

Well you know Mr. Satchel McVea was indeed a legend. He was the father of Jack McVea and he started many musicians in Los Angeles playing; he played for many of the social affairs of the white community at that time. He was the father of Jack McVea and he was one of the black musicians that refused to join the union. He had quite a bit of work at that time without being a member of the musicians union, so he sort of rebelled and I don't think during his whole career he was ever a member of either Local 767 which was the
"colored union," or later Local 47. [He was] quite an important man in early musical history of Los Angeles.

That's right, he had plenty work and if myself or Ash Hardy, didn't have a steady job, we'd call him up and he'd say, 'Oh, yes, you're not working this Saturday, okay I got a job for you. How about next Wednesday, are you doing anything?' I can remember that; we'd call him our ace in the hole.
Satchel McVea. I never knew his given name.
Isaac.
He was a banjo player, he lived on East 34th Street in Los Angeles. What else can you tell us about the moving picture?
It's pretty hard to remember exactly, because we did so many in those days and there were so many one day affairs. You did the work for that day and
then you'd wait for the next call or something like that.

I remember playing a picture called the Night Nurse, I think it was Colleen Moore; it's pretty hard to remember because we played of them, in fact I worked in more silent pictures than I worked in talking pictures.
Maybe a little later on in our interview we will touch on the talking movies.
All I can remember about the silent movies, one picture--I forgot the name of it now--I remember that because we had it the whole week.
Did you do any other playing during 1927 that you can recall? Or can you tell me anything about the musicians that you worked with?
At the time I worked on this set, we were working in San Bernadino and I had to come down here every
day to do the picture and then go back with Johnny Mitchell and play at night because we were playing a dance hall in San Berna- dino at night.
Who was with me--Ellis Wash I think.
Was he not a drummer?
Yes, he was a drummer.
Can you recall any of the other musicians that were working with you at this time?
We had a girl piano then, but I can't think of her name.
What about Mr. Sturdivant, [illegible], who I think inspired Dexter Gordon.
He's in here too.
Did he work with you at that time, or was it later on?
We worked sixteen months at the Burbank Theater in the pit.
Was that later on?
Yes, that was later, 1929.
We'll touch on Mr. Sturdivant later in our interview.

During the year 1927 I also played with Harry Southern's band, out at Belman's Open Air out in Widiam (phonetic spelling). I also played with Herb Williams who had a job up in San Francisco on the beach in San Francisco. Now I'm going into June, 1928.
Let me ask you just a couple more questions about 1927.

During this time--you mentioned San Bernadino, musicians making trips from San Bernadino to Los Angeles. Did the musicians play much in areas like San Luis, or Santa Barbara or up the coast during that time?
Not during that time, later on they did.

In San Bernadino we had kind of circuit up there; we lived up there. We played San Bernadino on Saturday night, the weekend; we'd go up to Hemet, down to Pomona, Riverside and around like that. That was during the summer of 1927 with Johnny Mitchell. I did that with him up until July and then I got with Harry Southern, with the open air dance.
Was that the club in Whittier? Was that in Whittier, California?
Just before you get to Whittier. It was right on Whittier Boulevard.
You had a pretty full 1927.
Oh, yes. I worked pretty steady all through those years; from one job I'd go right onto another. I had another open air dance in Culver City too.
Was that in '27 or '28?
That was in '28, I think.
Let's talk some about 1928.
In 1928 I joined Leon René's band, also at Belmon.
I think Mr. Leon René is the composer of that song, 'When the Swallows Come Back to Capistrano'.
Yes.
He had a brother by the name of Otis René.
That's right, and a cousin named Sam Beaumon; he had the drugstore.

I stayed with Leon from June to the holidays. We worked at the open air dance until it closed, then we went out to Spie'Iman's Nightingale (phonetic spelling) in Culver City. It had been closed and he
tried to reopen it and we went to the re-opening because he was bucking Frank Sebastian next door, and he had Miss Carolyn Snowden's review.
I think Miss Snowden was an outstanding woman musician at that time?
No, she was just a show producer. You're talking about the other Snow-- Valaida.
Were they related?
No, no. One was Snow and the other was Snowden.
I see.

Of course that job didn't last, he didn't make it go and so Leon didn't have much work and so the last job I had with him was on New Year's Eve, 1928/ After that I didn't play with him anymore because he didn't have any work.
Mr. Blakeney, tell us a little bit about the Sebastian Cotton
Club; Frank Sebastian, I think, is very significant.
Is that not where Bing Crosby and the trio that he was singing with once worked?
No, I don't think so.
I think you're talking about the Biltmore, also the Coconut Grove.
Did the Les Hite Orchestra work there for Frank Sebastian?
Oh, yes, sure Les worked there.
That was a pretty important club at that time.
It was the best job we had in Los Angeles. If you worked the Cotton Club, we couldn't get a better job, except the theaters. I think the Burbank Theater and the Follies Theater.
You also worked the Follies Theater?
I worked the Burbank; they were owned by the same man. The Dalton brothers.
Were these theaters both going during the late twenties?
That's right, they were both going.
And you played live music in the pit?
In the pit. Backing up the stage show, 85 people on stage.
'28 and '29, going into the thirties.

I stayed there from January 1929 to May 1930, in the pit, and the musicians were Parker Berry on trombone, Lee Gibson on drums, Sturdivant on first sax, Barnett on second sax, and Hugo Dandridge on third sax.
Big band.
On guitar we
had--I can't think of his name--and on bass dark-skinned boy, from Panama we had Sig Carter; he was a light-skinned fellow. We had twelve pieces.
That was considered a pretty big band in those days.
Oh, sure, that was a big show we had to back up.
Tell us a little bit about the Follies, on Main Street. Wasn't it on Main Street?
That's right, they both were on Main Street. The Follies was up at Fourth and Main and the Burbank was at Sixth and Main.
Tell us a little bit about the shows; what they were like.

Well, they were burlesque shows, you know, they had strippers and I can remember when Reb Spikes opened up the Follies, I was supposed to go with him. After Reb Spikes left, George Brown took it over around '28, and then
Dalton wanted to open up another burlesque because it was going so good up there, and that was the Burbank Theater at Sixth and Main. That's when I started with them, January, 1929.
That was, I consider, the hardest job I ever had and most responsible job I've ever had.
Were you playing continuously for the dances?
There were regulars; the show would be about an hour and then we'd have a break before the picture was going on. Three shows a day and four on Saturdays.
What do you think made it so difficult for you? Why was it such a hard job?
The music we had to play, it was all types of music, ballet music, overtures, marches, waltzes, clog dances and they had a chorus line of forty five girls.
That was in Los Angeles.

I was hired to play second trumpet and I was going to play under a famous circus man, he was well known all over the country for circuses and minstrel shows, and the first week his lip went out on him and so they moved me over to first chair, and they promoted him to get up and direct the band. First he was sitting down taking the cues from the piano player, so they gave him a stick with a light at the end of it so he could direct the band, because he was not only a good musician, he was a good writer and arranger, and they needed him.

You know that refutes the conception that many people have about jazz musicians as not being qualified to read the music, that you were saying that you had to play for many, many kinds of acts. You certainly had to be qualified.
Some say they had tough shows at the Cotton Club, because I played there with Caroline Snowden, but nothing was tougher than the burlesque show because they were all white.
All of the entertainers were white?
Oh, yes, the whole show was white.
Did they have any mixed bands at the time?
No.
The bands were all black?
All black. That's about all until 1930.
(Side A of Tape 1 ended at this point. Transcript will continue in accordance with Side B.)
(Side B of Tape 1 begins at this point.)

Mr. Blakeney, let's discuss 1930 in Los Angeles. What was the Los Angeles music scene like when you arrived from Chicago, and what areas did the black musicians work; what were their salaries, and their working conditions?
In the thirties the salaries weren't too large, working conditions were fair.
Was there a union at this time?
Oh, yes. Yes, there was a union.
Perhaps at this time there were two unions?
Oh, yes, a white union and a black union.
Was the black union yet at 17th and Central or was it located someplace else?
It was at 17th and Central.
It was, in the early thirties?
Yes. It was run in the thirties by Bailey.
Was that William Bailey? No, that was his brother, I think, who was the physician.
I don't remember no William Bailey. What was his first name? Ed Bailey.
Ed Bailey; right. I remember the name William Bailey because his brother was our family doctor.
Is that so? I can't recall a William Bailey.
Much of the activity, I believe, at that time was around 12th and
Central, between 12th Street and Ninth Street, they were important streets at the time and I think Lionel Hampton lived in that area.
He did; yes.
What were some of the names of the clubs at that time, Mr. Blakeney?
I'm trying to think now.
Did the Spike Brothers have a club at anytime?
Yes. I'm trying to think what they called it.
Was there a club, Mr. Blakeney, called the Hummingbird, in that area?
Yes.
Who were some of the musicians who played at the Hummingbird Club near Twelfth and Central?
Gene Wright on piano, Harley Brooks.
This was the time before the musicians had moved down towards

There were two very important gentleman, it seemed, called the Spikes Brothers, Johnny and Reb. Why were they so important, Mr. Blakeney, during this time and previously to 1930; the Spike Brothers, why were they so important to the music scene, and particularly to the black musicians?
Because of the songs they wrote, like "Someday Sweetheart" and others which became very popular back in those days.
Did they get employment for other musicians, within their band? Did people come to them to hire other musicians?
Yes, they did. They worked out in Huntington Park, I guess, with their own group and hired other musicians
but I worked out there myself with him for a little while.
Did the Spikes Brothers ever have a club of their own?
No, not that I can remember.
Their primary role then was as orchestra leaders and as/com-songposers?
Yes.
Many of the musicians at this time sort of gravitated around them is that correct?
Yes, it is, to an extent.

Huntington Park, the area that you just mentioned, was a long, long way away from the Twelfth and Central area. Approximately how much time can you recall, did it take, for you to get to a job? Considering that most of the musicians lived in the area of Ninth, Eleventh or
Twelfth Street. How long did it take for you to get to Huntington Park at that time? Oh, not long, twenty or thirty minutes.
I'm trying to think of some of the places we played. Other than Huntington Park, you're saying?
Yes.

Mr. Blakeney, your first recording experiences out West was with the Sonny Clay Plantation Orchestra; this we do know. In that orchestra were people like W.B. Woodland, Ernest Coycault, Leonard "Big Boy" Davidson, Louis Dobbs; some gentleman whose last name was Fitzgerald--do you recall his first name? He was a banjo player.
Fitzgerald?
Yes.
I don't remember him much as a banjo player, mostly on the
piano.

Oh? We had him listed here as being a banjo player, but perhaps he was a piano. There were also other musicians on the date with you at the time, such as William Calhoun and W. B. Woodman, who was the father of Coney and Britt Woodman. Britt Woodman was a fine tromonist who played for many years with Duke Ellington, and who at this time I believe is active in New York.
Tell us a little bit about the lesser known musicians, maybe like William Calhoun. He was a multi-reed player, right?
That's right.
Can you recall much about Mr. Calhoun?
Not too much.
Let's talk a bit more, Mr. Blakeney, about William Woodman, the father of Coney and Britt Woodman.
The old man, he
was a good musician on the trombone and the articulation, boys followed him and his style, on the trombone. He made a lot of fast passages on the trombone; he was famous for that.
Was Mr. Woodman also a barber?
Yes.
Several of the musicians during that time had jobs other than performing as musicians; is that right?
That's right, yes.
I can imagine that the music was indeed an outlet for them after performing some menial job during the day, I guess they looked forward to going to the gig that night to play; do you think so?
Yes.
Lionel Hampton was on the scene then and I know you recorded with him when you recorded with the Spikes Brothers.
That's right.
Tell us a little bit about Lionel. He's still going and just tremendous....
I had little difficulty in consoling him on the record, he was naturally loud, they didn't have a place to put him, and one of the directors said, put him out in the bowls.
Was that because he was so strong on the drums?
That's right.
He was not playing the vibes at this time?
No.
The drums overpowered the rest of the band.
That's right. The director made a remark, he said put him out in the bowls.
He was so powerful they thought well, he can't stay in here and record.
That's right.
Tell us some more about Lionel, who is indeed a legend.
He was powerful on the drums; he was what we called a noisy drummer.
Did he swing?
Yeah, he could swing.
Did Lionel ever have his own orchestra at this time? Did he have an orchestra in the early thirties?
No.
He was just digging around with the rest of the guys; is that right?
That's right.
You could recognize his unusual talent at this time?
Oh, yes.
About when do you recall him playing the vibes?
He started out around this time with the vibes.

Around that time Mr. Blakeney, there were several really talented and unusual women musicians; Mrs. Alma Hightower (phonetic spelling) was one, who later became a teacher of some outstanding students; Mrs. Loretta Butler, who was also a dancing teacher; and Miss Fannie (?) Benjamin, who is yet with us and playing.
Tell us a little bit about Mrs. Hightower; you did work with her on occasion?
Yes.
What do you remember most about her?
I remember she was very artistic and insisted on the musicians playing exactly as written.
She played several instruments. On the jobs that you worked with her, what instruments did she play?
All I can remember
She also played the drums and the trumpet, and several other instruments.
What about Mrs. Loretta Butler, who later became a dance teacher. She was on the scene then too.
That's right.
Can you remember Mrs. Butler?
Yes, I can remember her, as a very good pianist.
Was Mrs. Marian Sturdivant playing at this time, the wife of Mr. Sturdivant? Did she work much at this time?
Yes she did, she worked alot with us. She was very good too, a very good musician.
Mr. Blakeney, tell us a bit about the interaction between the male and the female musicians during this
time. What was the attitude of the men musicians towards the women?

The attitude then was that the woman pianist wasn't quite as strong as the men would like them to be, especially as the background, the left hand chords; it wasn't as good as the average man. A man understood more than the average woman.
(unintelligible)
Was this so with Mrs. Hightower and Mrs. Butler?
Yes.
Do you think that the men musicians were concerned as to whether or not they were male or female?
Some of the musicians were, they figured a woman pianist wasn't heavy enough, especially on the voicing of the cords.
At this time were there any women playing other instruments in the band, that you recall?
Not to any extent,
Mostly pianist?
Mostly pianist. I liked one that came up--I can't think of her name.
Was that Valaida Snow?
No.
Was Miss Snow ever in the California area, that you recall?
Yes, back in that time she was around, but mostly with shows that she was with.
She was like a specialty act?
Something like that, yes. Valaida Snow; I don't remember too much about her personally. I don't remember ever working with her.
Mr. Blakeney, I think before Prez Bailey, there was another person who was the first president of the colored
musicians union as it was called. Incidentally, I know the address there was 1710 South Central Avenue.
That person was from a very prominent family, the Johnson's. There were several school teachers in the family and he was a very outstanding man involved in politics also at the time.
Can you recall his first name?
He was the president before Edward Bailey.
Spencer Johnson.
Right.
Spencer Johnson; he had a son who was a musician also, Carl. The daughters were schoolteachers; Hilda, Gloria and one other daughter. He was the president prior to Mr. Bailey.
Mr. Blakeney, would you state for us, if you can recall, the attitude of the community towards the musician at that time; how was the musician looked upon by the non-professionals in the community?
Not so good. He was considered loud and unprofessional.
What was the level of respect for them in the community? Were they considered as professionals?
Yes, in some ways. Some of the musicians were.
I guess as today some were respected more than others?
That's right.
Some of those musicians were family men, with families, and were good family men.

We've spoken as to how the community felt about some of the musicians; what was the attitude of some musicians towards their peers, the stronger, more proficient players; how did some of the less skilled musicians look at them, and vice-versa?
Well, you take guys like Lionel, he was considered a rabble rouser. You'd see him around with some of
the lesser known musicians. He wasn't particular about who he ran with.
I can remember the time he was criticized for being out with a bunch he shouldn't have been.
This is what I had reference to, this kind of respect or disrespect; whatever you call it.
Were there the usual petty jealousies among the musicians?
Yes, there were in a way.
Leon used to critize Lionel about how he used to run around, the type of fellows he used to run around with, he shouldn't do it.
Was the name Leon?
Leon Heriford.
What did he play, Mr. Blakeney?
Saxophone. He was a fine musician, one of the finest during
that time, as a saxophone man. He had a pretty tone.
Did he ever speak to Lionel about it?
Oh yes, yes.
And what was his response if you can recall?
His response was it's not their concern who he runs around with on his days off.
It's his own business?
That's right.

Was there more of a fraternal feeling among the musicians, the welfare of their fellow musicians? Were physically they concerned about each other, about how they were getting along, if they had a job, about their circumstances at home? Was there a feeling of fraternity?
There was a feeling of fraternity among some of the musicians towards others. Sometimes Lionel would be

in the center of it because he was running around with different guys that he shouln't have, we thought because he was too decent to be running around with certain kinds of musicians. I thought that Lionel had a problem.
Was Mr. Hampton married to Gladys Hampton at this time?
I don't think he was married to her; no.
He was perhaps about one of the youngest in the group about that time; is that right?
That's right; yes. Him and Baby Lewis were about the same age, I guess.
Is that Baby Lewis?
Yes.
What did Baby Lewis play?
Drums, like Lionel.
Were they friends?
Oh, yes, with each other. Both of them were kind of eccentric on the drums; they played vibes.
Both of them were eccentric on the drums?
Yes. Also Baby Lewis was better than Lionel.
Baby Lewis was a contemporary of Lionel?
Yes; right.
During that time Mr. Blakeney, how did the musicians more or less entertain themselves? Was there any hanging out as we know it today after the gig?
Oh yes, we used to hang around certain places.
Were there after hours jam sessions?
Yes.
Can you remember some of the clubs where the guys used to hang out?
Some of them probably didn't hang out too long, perhaps like yourself you had to get home to wives.
That's right; yes.
You had a wife and one son, was it, Mr. Blakeney?
A daughter.
You had a wife and one daughter at that time?
That's right.
As we said previously, many of these musicians were very, very strong family men.
That's right.

Mr. Blakeney, about this time were many of the musicians interested in political picture of the day? I know from what I've read that most of the black musicians and many black people were Republicans during this time, up until about the time of the election of Roosevelt. Can you give us some idea as to the political
awareness or lack of awareness on the part of the musicians? You mentioned Lionel several times. I know he is yet a Republican, but most of them became Democrats, most of the black population.
During that time we leaned mostly towards the Democrats, as I remember. That was when Roosevelt was popular.

The name of Hearst, the first family was very and yet is very prominent in newspaper politicals, on the general scene; the Hearst family, William Randolph Hearst in California at that time. Mr. Hearst was very important in terms of finances, et cetera; do you have any memory of him at all?
He was a very conservative gentleman, as was the whole family.
He first started out with his newspapers, his editorial poli-
cies and everything, we considered him anti-black.
I think he was known as anti-black up until the time of his demise.
Maybe so; yes.
He was the grandfather of Patty Hearst that we've heard much about in recent years.

Did his attitude towards the black musicians effect where, how and when they worked? He had so much influence over the general picture of Los Angeles; did his strong anti-black feelings effect the black musician?
I would say no. We considered him anti-black, but he didn't care too much about the black race in his newspapers, as I remember now.
But you don't recall him preventing you from getting employment in certain places at the time?
No.
(End of Tape 1)
(Side A of Tape 2 begins at this point.)

During the mid thirties, after the election of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, there was a major social program, in addition to the social security program, called the WPA, or the Work Project Administration, and this program effected many musicians; can you tell me what you remember about the WPA, Mr. Blakeney?
There's not much I can remember about the WPA, I didn't participate in the WPA too much because--I don't know.
You just didn't?
I just didn't.
Where were some of the concerts held? Were there concerts held by the WPA bands?
Yes, I remember a concert at the union hall at meetings.
At the musician's
Yes.
Did the people in the community come out to these free concerts?
Yes.

The WPA also touched other artists, not just musicians. There were singers all involved in the WPA program; it was geared to the low income persons at that time who was out of work, so I would think that many of the black musicians probably participated; is that right?
Yes; that's the way I see it, yes.

Mr. Blakeney, as you probably know--I'm sure you know, having been one of the pioneers of the Central Avenue era, there has been much, much misinformation about Central Avenue during the late thirties into the forties and fifties. Kindly brief us on the real Central Avenue, the real Central Avenue scene.
Let us know about when the black musicians started to ignite the area with their vibrant bands and shows, and who were some of these black musicians that were very active during this time.
What time would this be now?
This would be the late thirties into the forties. Central Avenue was hot.
Late thirties into the forties--that's when the Alabam was popular. There was a piano player back in those days, Marie Dickerson.
Marie Dickerson was also I think the first licensed black woman aviatrix in the State of California.
Yes, I think so.
And her name is now Marie Coker, she was married to the late trombonist Henry Coker.
That's right.
She was an entertainer; is that right?
That's right.
Who were some of the other instrumentalists? Was Nat King Cole on the scene then?
I guess he was, yes. So was Alton, so was your dad back in those days.
Alton Redd. What about the Royal Brothers?
Back in those days they were pretty popular too, they were coming up.
Was that Marshall and Ernie?
That's right. I didn't watch Ernie too much.
He came on later. Do you remember C.P. Johnson?
Oh yes, I remember
C.P.
Can you remember some of the members of his band? He played at the Club Alabam.
That's right. No, I can't recall any of the members of his band.
Kirk Bradford--do you remember Kirk Bradford?
Kirk Bradford played alto sax.
That's right.
Buddy Collette perhaps in the early forties, he was a member of the C.P. Johnson orchestra. Johnson was a bongo player, very flamboyant.
Yes.
T-Bone Walker,was he in there? Did he come in and out of the Club Alabam?
I don't remember.
You don't remember
Not too well. Back in those days I might remember him.
Did T-Bone Walker come on in the forties perhaps, more closer to World War II?
I'm trying to remember when did he come on.

Can you remember the names of any of the clubs other than the Club Alabam, which was adjacent to the Dunbar Hotel, which is now a historical monument-- historical landmark, in Los Angeles. This is the hotel that was owned by Dr. Summerville, the black dentist.
Yes; I remember him.
The black entertainers and musicians could not live in downtown Los Angeles at this time. Was there the Last Word? That was there too.
/ Where was this located?
It was on Central Avenue.
Your dad can remember all that now. I can see him.
Who is that?
Your dad, Alton.
Yes, he was very active in that time. He hired quite a few musicians during the time.
Leonard Davidson, "Big Boy", was with him during this time thereabout and he continued to do so throughout this period until about World War II, when the whole scene started to branch out a bit more.
Do you remember Ivie's Chicken Shack?
Yes, I do.
Do you remember the lady that owned it? Tell me something about her.
Ivie owned it;
didn't she? Yes she did. Who was she?
She was a singer and became very popular.
What was her last name?
Ivie Anderson.
Is that the lady who sang with Duke Ellington?
That's right; same lady.
She had a chicken shack on Central Avenue?
That's right.
The forty-four-hundred block; that was called Vernon Avenue?
Yes.
I've been told that Art Tatum was in the area and playing at a place called Lovejoy's in those late thirties and early forties; do you recall this club?
No, I don't remember Lovejoy's.
You don't remember Lovejoy's?
I don't remember the club; no. I remember the area; it was kind of popular in that time, yes.

This Ivie's Chicken Shack, she was a great vocalist, Ivie Anderson, who appeared with the Duke Ellington Orchestra for many, many years. This was about the time that Duke Ellington brought his orchestra to Los Angeles to appear at the Mayon (phonetic spelling) Theater in a show called Jump for Joy.
Yes; I remember that.
Good afternoon, once more we are in the comfortable setting of the home of Mr. Andrew Blakeney in Pasadena, California on June 24, 1982.

Due to circumstances beyond our control, that being Mr. Blakeney's sudden serious illness just a few hours after our last interview, we must regress chronologically with Mr. Blakeney as he continues his oral history interview.
His recovery has been marvelous for which we are all so very grateful. We now begin with the year 1935 and his experiences as a member of the Lionel Hampton Orchestra in Los Angeles.
I would like to take time out here and go back a few years, when I was with Lionel Hampton.
We had a very strong band, all experienced musicians. All had their homes and families here in Los Angeles. The musicians were such as Paul Howard, Lloyd Allen,
Red Mack, Pee Wee Brice, Buster Wilson, and others.
Can we comment on a couple of those musicians in the band, Mr. Blakeney?
Was that the Emerson Scott who was such a fine alto saxophonist, and vocalist?
That's right.
There was Paul Howard; was he a bandleader at one time?
That's right, he was very famous with the Quality Serenaders way back in the early twenties. I remember that, with Leon Herriford--and I can't think of the lady's name now.

Lionel wouldn't, or couldn't, pay salaries that would enable us to take care of our families, and at the same time take care of our expenses on the road, so by July most of us quit. Most of us were replaced by younger and inexperienced musi-
cians. Among those were Don Byas, who later became famous all over America and Europe. At that time I was back in Los Angeles playing casuals, small jobs at Depression wages.
Depression wages you say? About what was that, Mr. Blakeney? What were the wages about that time?
Well, I was making $17.50 for seven days work.
A week.
Was that the union scale?
No, the union scale was much more than that, but we didn't—
That's what you were making?
They allowed us to get what we could.
Right.
In September I received a job to go to Honolulu--this is
at the same time that I was working on that $17.50 job.
That was a new offer?
New offer.
This offer was from Bernard Banks, the pianist who was taking a group to Honolulu to play in a dancehall there.
Wasn't Bernard Banks the brother of Buddy Banks?
That's right.
Who played saxophone and later piano?
That's right.
I was attracted because the money was good and the job was steady.
How was that good? What do you mean?
$35.00 a week
That was a far cry from the $17.50; wasn't it? And Hawaii too.
I took my wife with me and I left our daughter with her

grandmother in Los Angeles. After three months, my wife's mother passed and she came back to Los Angeles for the funeral and then she had to bring our daughter back with her. She was only eleven years old at that time; this is 1936, in January.

Our band went over very big in dance halls Honolulu at the / and so our boss took advantage of it and booked us on private jobs. We didn't care about that because we were still getting our $35.00 a week.
You made some extra too then; didn't you?
He gave us a little extra.
Our personnel was Henry Coker (unintelligible spelling), Kirk Bradford, Leon Scott, Bill Winston; those were musicians who were famous back in Chicago in the thirties.
The name Henry Coker,
the late Henry Coker, later had a stint with the Count Basie Band; didn't he?
That's right, he worked ten years with Count Basie.
And also married Marie Dickerson that we mentioned earlier.
That's right, Marie Dickerson, she was a pilot.
Yes, an aviatrix.
We played there until the bombing of Pearl Harbor.
That was December 7, 1941.
That's correct. They closed all the dancehalls so we were out of work. So most of the musicians got jobs in defense.
In Hawaii?
In Hawaii. So they were told that they couldn't quit until the war was over, but I knew that they were freezing the jobs in
defense, so I got me a job driving a cab.
Driving a cab was not considered defense work?
No. It was my own cab and I wasn't working for anybody, and I could leave anytime.

By June of '42, I had transportation accommodations with permission to leave with my family. After a dangerous crossing of the Pacific on an Army transport ship, with three warships escorting her to protect us from Japanese subs.
Did the government give you permission to come over on that ship?
Oh yes. They gave us notice, they'd give us twenty-four hours notice, to stay by the phone, have money ready for your tickets; that was the order we got, see.
That was quite an experience; that was a very dangerous time,
Yes.
It was funny how the ship had to zig zag to try and duck the submarines.
The Japanese submarines were in the area; is that it?
Yes.
After eight days we arrived in San Francisco. I sent my wife to Los Angeles and I continued on to Chicago because I thought maybe I could go back there and re-settle.
I was there only one week, enough to convince me that Chicago was not the place.
After Hawaii and California, you had to come back?
That's right.
So I rushed back to San Francisco; I was there three months.
Did you work any during that time in San Francisco?
No. I think I had about a half a dozen gigs. Finally I figured that wasn't the place for me and I ended up back in Los Angeles, in October, 1942.
I found a job playing my horn immediately; that's when I was with Carl Johnson.
Yes, you were with the Carl Johnson Orchestra.
Carl Johnson was the son of Spencer Johnson, who was at one time the president of the then Local 767.
That's correct.
The 'all-Colored' local.
How long did you stay with him?
Oh, maybe a couple of months. I was with him at the time that I went to work at the shipyard.
Tell us about your experience with him.
Working at the shipyard everyday and getting home at six o'clock at night and had to be at work at eight and work until one o'clock in the morning.

One time Carl was knocking off the band and instead of me playing, I was sitting there asleep. So Carl let me go; he said it was better if you go because it was too much for you working daytime and night too. It tickled me (laughter).
Like burning the candle at both ends.
Anyway--
But then I guess at that time a lot of musicians were working in the defense plants and playing gigs at night.
Oh yes.
April of the next year, which is 1943 now, C.L. asked me if I wanted to work in his band, because the trumpet player he was was George Arndorff--do you know him?
George Arndorff, yes; didn't he at one time work with Kid Ory?
No, he worked with the Quality Serenaders.
Oh, Mr. Paul Howard.
And Les Hite too. I guess you remember when he was with Les Hite.
C.L. Burke was quite a personality; wasn't he?
Oh yes.
He was well known in the L.A. area.
Yes; he liked to play Hawaiian type music. He fact he was featured on the steel guitar.
Polynesian.
Yes. Then he played a lot of Latin tunes.
I think his complexion was such that he could have presented himself as Polynesian, perhaps.
Yes, and he did, the way he wore his hair; he kind of looked like a Hawaiian.
I stayed with C.L. three and a half years altogether.
What was the name of the club where you worked?
Bell Tavern.
Gardena, California. Was that the club where they had the famous chorus line and all these dancing girls?

That's right. Blufield and Greeley had the floor show, because I had played with him before that at the Cotton Club back in the thirties, at the time when Duke Ellington came out there and played a short time and we followed them. / That was in 1934.
And you worked with at the Bell Tavern C.L. Burke from 1943 to 1946; is that correct?
That's correct.
Musicians went on jobs and worked for a long time like that, in those times, if they had a good gig; they spent several years there, unlike the later two weeks here and four weeks here.
That's right. I liked it because I wanted a steady job.
Right; take care of your family.
I was able to get good credit too being on a job for a long time. That's when I bought my first home.
Really? That's interesting because I'm sure it was difficult for musicians then, even more difficult than it is now for them to get credit.
It certainly was.
I have been told that oftentimes the club owners would vouch for a musician, to help them establish their cre-
dit and buy homes and so forth. I got credit on my own because I had been working at Bell Tavern well over a year when I applied for it.
And that's when you bought your first home?
That's right.
Do you remember where that home was? I bet you never forgot it.
Oh, sure. 121 17 Parmalee.
That was in the Watts area; wasn't it?
That's it. Willowbrook.
That's just a little east of the Watts area; isn't it?
A little south. 122nd and Parmalee. Imperial was the dividing line of Watts, and just below that was the
county, and Willowbrook started I think, around 118th Street.
That area still has some very comfortable homes.
I sold my home in 1940--no, '50.
You sold your home there in 1950?
It must have been '61.

I stayed with C.L. Burk three and a half years, ending at the Club Alabam on Central Avenue, L.A. The stay at the Alabam was very short due to the fact we were working for Curtis Mosby who was trying to stage a comeback in the nightclub form.
Mr. Curtis Mosby was very well known for his wheeling dealings in the area. I think he was the brother of Red Mack, who was--Mrs. Hightower taught Red Mack and Curtis Mosby was his brother.
I didn't know that. I knew he had two or three brothers, one of them Evans Mosby; you know him, don't you?

I've heard of him. Maybe we'll come back to that later, because their mother--the mother of Red Mack was a very well know real estate person during that time. He had nightclubs in the area, as I've been told, and also had his financial difficulties,which you are reiterating now.
I think you have the two nightclub owners mixed up.
Perhaps I do.
Curtis Mosby had the Alabam and Red Mack's brother owned the Plantation.
What was his name?
His name was Mosby--Morris was their last name, you know. I can't think of his name.
Perhaps it will come to you--to the two of us.
Red Mack, his name was McClure Morris, and his brother ran the Plantation out there on 107th and Central Avenue. Those are the two night-clubs I got mixed up.
The Plantation was further out on Central, way, way out.
107th And Central.
And the Club Alabam was in the heart of everything, on 42nd Place.
There is no relation between Curtis Mosby....
I know the gentleman's name--it was Joe Morris.
That's right. That's Red Mack's brother.
Right; and he owned the Plantation. I stand corrected, Mr.Blakeney.
That's right.
Was he involved in the Last Word nightclub?
He probably was because he was a tap dancer. He still is a tap dancer.
After we left Curtis, C.L.'s band broke up and I went to work for the board of education.
Los Angeles Unified School District.
Correct; I stayed with them twenty-one years.
But you also did some playing then though.
Well yes, after I started working with Ory, because it was about eight months after I left C.L. before I started with Ory.
For just about eight
you worked for L.A. Unified Schools?
That's right.
And then reactivated your music with Kid Ory?
That's right.
Tell us about that.
In May 1947, I didn't play a single job, from October to May. About the middle of May, Kid Ory and his guitarist, Bud Scott--
The legendary Kid Ory.
--came to my house and asked me if I wanted to join their band.
Mr. Blakeney, were you living on Parmalee then?
I was still living on Parmalee--12117 Parmalee Avenue. I said yes even though I had never played any dixieland band. Ory was quite successful in his comeback as a leader
and he had a lot of work lined up.
After twenty-five years playing music, the public had just begun to recognize me as a trumpet player.
Overnight star, after twenty-five years.
(Laughing)
In spite of my best trumpet playing days was before I started playing with Ory.
My work with Ory was playing casuals, clubs, movies and recordings.
Who were some of the other musicians in that band?
There was Joe Darenbourg, Montudie Garland, Bud Scott, Ram Hall--
He was the drummer?
He was the drummer.
Did Alton ever work with you?
Not with Ory; we
With Ory.
With Ory, no. I'll get to Alton pretty soon.
All right.
I was playing records with Ory, recording, for two years, ending with a six-month stand a the Beverly Cavern.
That was a club out on Beverly Boulevard?
Beverly Boulevard. This is 1949 now.
They used to feature a lot of the dixieland bands in that club.
That's right.
A lot of the college kids would go there, L.A. City College.
That's right. What's his name, a jazz fan, Floyd Levin?
Floyd Levin and his
wife, Lucille.
They used to come there before they were married; they were just youngsters.
They're really well known as jazz lovers.
In the meantime I was working daytime with the board of education.
Ory stayed at the Cavern three or four months with Teddy Buckner in my place after I left.
When did you leave?
In July, 1949.
Do you mind me asking, were you just sort of exhausted at the time?
I was kind of exhausted, kind of frustrated because I didn't like Ory's style of playing. The music he was playing was very monotonous, playing the same old New Orleans tunes night

to playing
after night. I'm used a variety of tunes,
anything and everything.
This is a more dixie-land repetoire.

That's right,
and not many tunes at that.
We left as friends anyway, and
he hired Teddy Buckner to take my place and
they stayed there about three months after
I left, and he left suddenly and the boss
called me up, and the personnel of this band
that I took back into the Beverly Cavern following Kid Ory?
was Eldridge Cooper on piano, Reginald
Jones on bass,--
Jonesy?

Jonesy.
Alton Redd on drums, William
Woodman on trombone, and I first hired
Seymour Taylor on clarinet. After he was
there one week I got a fine clarinet man
named Albert Nicholas.

He went to Europe
and stayed a while.
We stayed there a while, of course we couldn't pull in the crowd like Kid Ory, who had a name. Then we went from there over to--what's that club?
What was the name of that club where you took the band after you left the Cavern?

The 400 Club. On 6th and (inaudible). We had almost the same personnel. This time it was Alton Redd on drums, Eldridge Cook on piano, "Streamline"; that was his first time playing dixieland, and a clarinet player by the name of Phil Gomez, a Mexican boy.
We stayed there a while and then I went back to the Beverly Cavern and I had another fine band over at the Cavern when I went back. Cook was on piano, Montudie on bass.
Of course that was the legendary Montudie Garland.
That's right. On clarinet we had Bob McCracken,
a white guy; and on trombone we had Warren Smith, who used to be with the Bobcats.
