That's Bob Crosby's Bobcats?
Yes. We stayed there until the joint changed hands; he sold it to a man named Al Dietz.
I can remember the night that he took over, it was on a Saturday night.
Why don't you tell us about that experience.

Well, I didn't know whether he was going to keep us or what so I went up to him and asked him, what about us. I said, do you intend for us to stay? He said well, if the crowd stays like this don't worry about it.
That was nice to hear, wasn't it?
Yes. We stayed there for a while.
That was quite a nice little run there, wasn't it?
It was; yes. There's something I wanted to say about my private life right in there too; I have it all down.
That was around 1955. You were still with the board of education?
That's right. Working every day and every night.
Did you want to say something about your family?

Yes. I lost my wife in 1953, in December; that's the mother of my daughter. The next year I married again and ten years later I lost her. I lost my wife, the next year I married again and in 1964 I lost her.
So you lost the two wives?
Yes. Now I'm married to the most beautiful woman in the world. We have been married sixteen years, the most happiest years of my life.
What's her name?
Ruth.
She's a very lovely hostess, and a fine person.

During the sixties I was playing other types of music besides jazz. I was a member of a number of marching bands, concert bands, even a community symphony orchestra. Most of my work at that time was with the Urban Concert Band.
Was that Percy McDavid's band?
No, we had two bands at that time. This is Millard Lacy.
Oh, yes.
I was solo trumpet player in that group for a number of years.
Wasn't Percy McDavis a contemporary--he was a contemporary of Lacy; didn't they have the bands going at the same time?
Yes we did. We played classics, and marches.
Well you know to get back to the marching situation, as they do with the marching bands in New Orleans, or was that a little different?
Yes, it was a little different. New Orleans was mostly jazz.
You played the John Philip Sousa and so forth?

Oh yes. I was a favorite trumpet player among the marching bands in those days because I could remember those tunes note for note and I didn't have to be walking down the street trying to read as I was playing.
"Our Director," was that a famous march?
"Stars and Stripes Forever."
Were these bands active in the community in the Sixties?
Oh, yes, the Elks band, that's when I first started out.
Fraternal organizations?
Yes.
I was with the Elks band, the Shriners Band, the Letter Carriers Band.
And you still played your jazz gigs and still worked for L.A. Unified School District?
That's right.
What an experience you had.
I retired in 1964.
From L.A. Unified School District?
Yes. This is

eight months before I lost my third wife. After my retirement from the board of education in 1964, I stayed home to take care of my wife who was ill at the time. This is February, 1964, and that lasted until October '64, when she passed. After she passed, I took two or three trips to kind of get over my grieving. The first one I went to Chicago to visit my sister and then I came back. At that time it was near the holidays and I had a couple of gigs during the holidays. In the first part of January I wanted to go to Mexico City. I've never been to Mexico before--I mean deep Mexico. So I drove my car alone to Laredo, Texas; that's right on the line of Mexico. I parked my car in the garage, took the train to Mexico City and I was there for about two weeks. While I was there, I met an entertainer who was down there visiting,
Marie Dickerson. She just happened to be there and we had a nice little time reminiscing with each other.
I didn't stay long but she was still there, she had been down there for some time before I got there.
I understood she lived in Mexico for several years.
So I came back after about ten days I guess and on my way way to the border to get my car and drove to New Orleans. I had a lot of friends in New Orleans.
I know you couldn't resist playing down there.

Well, I didn't stay long the first time because I was on my way to my old hometown which was in Mississippi which is about five or six hours drive from New Orleans. I stayed there for about two weeks and then I went back to New Orleans and stayed in New Orleans for about
two weeks. That's when I met some old friends and went down to Preservation Hall and that's when I first met George Lewis.
Was he the first leader of that Preservation Hall band?
I can't say whether he was the first leader, but he was one of the most popular.
What instrument did he play?
Clarinet. The night I went down there I was escorted down there by an old friend of mine, in fact he used to work at Disneyland on the Mark Twain, a saxophone player, I don't even remember his name.
Polo--
That's right.
Barnes.
Polo Barnes; that's right.
Polo Barnes was very nice to me
while I was there. He took me to his house and his wife made a fried chicken dinner for me.
So we went down to Preservation Hall, Polo and I, and George Lewis was there with a combo, four pieces; a clarinet, trombone and piano and drums.
George asked us to sit in and so I sat in one set--
At Preservation Hall?
At Preservation Hall; and after that set the boss came up and said, put that fellow to work. They didn't have a trumpet player.
I was just down there visiting and so naturally I worked that night and I got paid for it.
Anyway, so much for that.
You didn't accept the offer to remain with them?
Oh no, no. He did offer, he said come down and I'll
give you a place to stay. I didn't want to live in New Orleans. I had my own home out here.
This is in '65 now, about February, when I got back to Los Angeles.
That was about 1965.
Perhaps you had somewhat of a new role at that time? What did you venture into at that time, Mr. Blakeney?
Later on that year, later, I think around December, I got into a new venture.

My niece, who used to be club owner out in Milwaukee, wanted to open up a place out here, and she couldn't get a license for it because she got in trouble with the IRS back there, and she asked me, she said I want to open this place but I want you to get the license for me. I agreed, not knowing what I was in for.
She said I need some more money, I think if you lend me a thousand dollars I
think I can make it. So I said I'll let you have the thousand dollars.
This is your niece?
This is my niece. When it ended up, she needed five-thousand dollars. Well, still didn't know what I was in for, so she opened the place under my name, I'm the license holder.
What's the name of the club?
The Sip 'n Beer.
In Pasadena?
Altadena.
Not too far from here.
Right.

And later on I found out that I was responsible for anything that happened, if somebody breaks a leg they can sue you, because your name is on the license. I took it over from my niece and I ran it myself, because I was responsible and I had the most money in it.
December, 1961 we opened up, we had to do some remodeling and change around. All we did was open the doors and the people just lined up to come in, with no advertising or anything.
Was that '64 or '61?
'65. I was the first colored man in business up in that area.
In Altadena.
The only other business up there was a barber shop and after I opened up there came a chicken shop and a rib shop.
Like a typical black community.
In the meantime I kept on playing gigs, if anybody called me for a gig I'd make it, I'd get somebody to run the place for me.
What did you like most about running a small nightclub?
This wasn't a nightclub.
A tavern?
Yes. Like the Chicago style neighborhood tavern.
What did you like most about it? I'm going to ask you what you didn't like.
It was just the people I liked, just seeing so many different people coming in. I liked it, I told my wife I'd kind of like to go back in business. She said oh no, you're doing it without me.
It finally got a little rough.
Well, in terms of being a businessman and being on the other not side of the spectrum and/being an entertainer per se, what did you find unusual?
It is quite a difference. All the years before that I was working on the other side of the bar. This
As the owner.

As the owner.
You have to watch everything;
you have to watch the outgoing and the in-
coming and the first thing, I was independent
of the income of that, because I had my in-
come already made at that time. I had the
pension and we had the rental property and
the money we made--I better stop here and
say from my private life again--this present
wife I married in '66.

When you right in
the middle of that business?

Yes, I only had
it a year.
I immediately made her a partner,
I immediately made her go through the same
thing that I had to go through to put her
name on the license. That's a hassle to
get an alcoholic license in California. You
don't know what you have to go through.
And as I told you when I would lay off from a gig I'd lose money, especially on a Saturday night; that's my getaway night.
What did she think about the nightclub business?

She didn't like it, because she was a professional woman. She was a piano teacher. When we married she had about a dozen scholars, teaching piano. I don't think she had a scholar since. (Laughing) I made a bargirl out of her.

At that time in California I don't think--even though your name was on the license--you clarify this for us. If a woman's name was on a license during the sixties in California, could she work behind the bar?
Yes, if her name was on the license.
But if her name was not on the license she was not allowed behind the bar.
That's right.
It was then, but it's changed now.
I know.
She being the owner yes, she could be behind the bar.
So you made her a bargirl.
I made a bargirl out of a professional piano player (laughing). The crowds began to get rough.
You got a bad element.
A bad element starting coming in and it ran my good customers away. I had good customers, people from church were coming in. (laughs)
Good Methodists.
Anyway, we went throught it and a profit was made.
How was the business? Did you do good?
It was good, we made a good profit the first three or four
years. My wife and I would just take off and take a trip, because we didn't need the money.
A lot of people in business, they go to the cash register and give the wife to go to the grocery store; well, I didn't have to do that.
You were in a very fortunate position that you had worked with the L.A. Unified School District and you had a retirement and other additional income.
That's right, which I could live on.
I was the only one up there where the delivery man didn't wait for his pay, all he had to do was sign. I was the only one, because all the rest of the places had to pay cash before he would leave.
The black population was very small at this time, wasn't it? There weren't very many blacks in Altadena at that time, in the early sixties?

Well, not too many, because we bought the place from a white guy and the reason he sold it was because the neighborhood was changing. That's why I didn't have to advertise because the negroes still living there didn't go in there as long as a white man owned it.
When I opened it here they come.
Yes, they were very glad to have some place to go and socialize.
I let my help off on Sundays, on Sunday my wife and I would run it ourselves, just the two of us on a Sunday.
You'd run it on Sunday?
Yes.
A lot different from running a club nowadays, isn't it? This was what, twenty years ago. Things have changed so much.
This was '65,
Are there any taverns now in the area?
There was another one on the same block I was, which was still owned by white.
Is it still there now?
It's still there now, but a colored boy is operating it now. My old place is still there too, but somebody else has it. We did so well that after two years we bought the property.
Did you lease it out or did you sell it subsequently?

I ran it for six years; I ran it from '65 to '71, then I leased it out for another year and then the second year that was renting it from me got slow in his pay and somebody suggested why don't you go back and open it and I said no, I had enough and so I just locked the
And you sold it?
I sold everything, the land and everything.
I can understand that, because Pasadena, Altadena, there were rigid racial restrictions for many, many years.
That's all.
Would you like to elaborate on that?
Well, knowing musicians, to hire bargirls and janitors and handymen around the place was enough than to have a musician on my payroll. I was a little bit too smart for that.
By this time with all your years of experience as a musician,
you had really learned? That's right.
You didn't want to venture hiring musicians and all the upkeep.
I knew the business inside out, from both sides of the bar. We were glad to get out in 1972, '73, when I really got out.
You had a very long, active, wonderful life.
When the business began to get rough a lot of my friends over there, your father and Lacy and Woodman and all of them, they began to worry about me. Owning a bar is kind of a dangerous business.
You know, the musicians really sort of had a fraternal feeling, they were concerned about the families, individuals. I could understand that.
I remember one time, Marvin Johnson--do you know Marvin Johnson?
Yes I do, a saxophonist.
And George Arndorf came by to see me one Sunday afternoon, the place was just packed. The Clef Club was meeting at Lucas' house.
Don Lucas.
Yes. Not far from where I had my business. So they came by just to say hello to me, I was so busy running back and forth they said, 'Okay I see you're busy, we'll see you later.'
Marvin Johnson was a fine saxophonist too, wasn't he?
He was. I think the first job he and Charlie--him and Charlie Jones was a team, you know, Marvin Johnson and Charlie Jones-- do you know Charlie Jones.
There was a Charles
Martin too.
Charlie Jones, from Rene's band when I first started.
With the now late Leon René.
Charlie left early--Charlie Jones worked out of the Bell Tavern too.
What did he play?
Saxophone, tenor sax. Marvin played the alto and Charlie played the tenor.
Charlie left early, I think it was in the forties, he left and went to --he and his wife-- Sacramento/and had a funeral parlor in Sacramento.
Mortician?
Mortician; yes.
Marvin played locally for many years.
He worked out of the Bell Tavern with us. He was in defense
His wife still lives here in Los Angeles, Iola Johnson.
I saw her not too long ago at the Clef Club Christmas party. Your mother was there.

You might mention the Clef Club. I know it was co-founded by Lee Gibson and you'll excuse the personal references in this interview, but I was the daughter of Alton Redd, and they founded that Clef Club.

I can remember the beginning of the Clef Club, it started as just a little private party. It was during the holidays and me and my wife had been south and we got back that morning and my niece was taking care of my house for me. She said she had a message and they want you to come to a party tonight. Lee Gibson invited me to come to his house.
Was it on 25th Street?
He had moved, he was on the west side then.
I didn't go to the party because we were tired, we just got in and I didn't go to the party, but that was the beginning of the Clef Club. That was in 1956.

I think the Clef Club was composed of all black musicians that belonged to Local 767, prior to 1940, and once more you'll forgive my personal inference, but I was made a member, an honorary member of the Clef Club approximately three years before my father's passing. I carried him to a club meeting once--
I remember that, he was in a wheelchair.
Absolutely. I haven't been able to keep that up because of my other activities, but I felt very honored. He was always a very benevolent

man and concerned about other people, and I think this organization was formed to act as an arm for the families and the musicians as they had their significant problems and so forth and it became a very kind of social thing; and it's still very active and a fine organization.
Let me say this about your father. When I lost my daughter's mother, Alton come and stood with me for days and helped me arrange the funeral and everything; I'll never forget that.
That was very typical of him.
And then when I lost my next wife he came right into this house and he was one of the pallbearers.
Okay, we've talked about your experiences after you left L.A. Unified School District, primarily your experience as a club owner, all of the "fun"
you had.

How long was it after you sold the property and were no longer running your tavern that you became involved with the Legends of Jazz? Would you like to talk about that now or is there something that you'd like to say?
Well my next activity after closing my business was with the Pasadena senior citizen center.
That was around 1972.
'72 or '73. It might have been '73.
Were you playing?
No, no.
I wanted to be active in something and so I went down there and told them that I wanted to join. They said we have some positions which are all no pay.
Volunteer work.
Volunteer work.
They asked what I was interested
in and I said I'm interested in travelling; well, we'll make you a travel host and so I was a travel host down there for about three months.

Anyway, I was behind the desk selling tickets to people who wanted to make trips, and then when they take these trips I was the host on the bus. I was the head man on the bus; I'd tell them what to do, where to get off, stop here and you have twenty minutes rest and things like that.
That didn't last very long, until I got an offer to go with the Legends of Jazz, which I'll tell you about later.
You're a very versatile gentleman.

Well, they liked me down there, they hated to see me leave because I had to sign receipts for all the money I take in and I had a pretty good handwriting and they liked that. I was decent and I was dressed up.
You'd run a business, you had to handle the money.
During that time I was working with a white band from Huntington Beach, called the South Frisco Jazz Band and I worked out there six months with them just weekends.
In Huntington Beach?
In Huntington Beach, a pizza parlor.
You drove from Pasadena down to Huntington Beach?

That's right, for six months, every Friday and Saturday night. Later on that year they got a job at a nightclub called Club New Orleans, / and I stayed with them for eight months. While we were there--this is 1972--right after I left the senior citizens, our first night out there was the night that Nixon got elected, there was a special party that night, an election night party they called it. 1972,
November.
This was after you were no longer a host at the senior citizens?
That's right. That was our opening night and we stayed there on that job from November to June, eight months.
Another long stretch.
While we were there this drummer, English drummer from English came in and asked me if I wanted to join his band because he wanted to organize an old timers band to travel.
What is his first name?
Barry Martyn. I never turned down anything in life so I told him yes. He said well, I haven't got all my men together yet, but you're one I'll count on. I asked Montudie, and I asked Joe Darensbourg.
Was he just in the

Yes--no, he made his home here I think. He first brought his own band over here, an English band and they couldn't make much of a headway with them so he just got rid of them and went and organized a black band of old timers.
He really wanted to get to the roots, the real thing.

Anyway, we started rehearsing, this is November now, November, 1972, and so the first of the year we started rehearsing, we'd go out to union everyday. The guys would be laughing at us, look at those old guys, they sure sound like heck.
With Montudit and Darensboug you couldn't have sounded like heck.
We were kind of passé, old timers playing old time music.
Everybody always laughed about dixieland music anyway.
So this was in spring and we rehearsed all that summer and so our first job was a tour to go back east. We were supposed to go to Europe on tour.

Let's talk about your experiences with the Legends Of Jazz, after your rehearsing here in Los Angeles at Local 47 and your initial engagements with this group, and they were indeed legends. Mention to us once more first of all the personnel in that band.
The personnel with the Legends was 'Montudie' Garland on bass, Louis Nelson on trombone, Joe Darensbourg on clarinet, myself on trumpet, Barry Martyn on drums, and Alton Purnell on piano.
Is that group still pretty much in tact with the same kind of personnel?
It's changed
some since then. Louis Nelson isn't a regular with the band anymore; he comes in every once in a while.
What did he play?
Trombone.
Purnell is still with the band, and myself I'm supposed to be with the band if I ever get back to work.
I'm sure you will. We're just so happy that you're up and about again.
That's about all of the originals of the band. Joe Darensbourg is not with the band anymore, he got tired of travelling.
Mr. Martyn.
He's still there.
And Montudie is passed on.
Who took his place?
Morris, Adolphus Morris.
He's from Los Angeles,
isn't he?
Yes, he lives
(inaudible)
(Side B of Tape 2 ended at this point.)
(Tape 3 begins)
--Clyde Bernhardt on the trombone took Louis Nelson's place.
For the most part the personnel has been pretty stable.
You say Barry more or less rediscovered you when you were playing on that engagement out in Orange County; is it?
That's right.
And asked you to join him.
That's right.
How long was it before the band became organized after your initial contact with him?

Well we started rehearsing a couple of months later; this was near the holidays of '72, around December, and we started rehearsing the next year, around February or March, around in there. We rehearsed up to our next tour
which was in September. I can remember we were supposed to go to Europe with this tour, but Europe was cancelled so we just made this trip.
You went up to New England; is that right?

Our first stop was a ski lodge in Wisconsin; Kaybee, Wisconsin, a ski lodge. We played there a few days and then we went to Minneapolis and played a club there called the Emporium of Jazz. Mendota, Minnesota.
Were there any significant incidents or anything unusual about these first engagements?

Well, the first engagement the only incident was we travelled by car from Chicago to Kaybee, Wisconsin and we had to stop overnight; we couldn't make it all in one day, so we stopped at some town in Wisconsin, right near Madison. It was cold but it wasn't
snowing so we parked our car right outside the motel and the next morning when we woke up we couldn't see the car because it was all covered with snow. This was February; can you imagine.

Anyway, we made it from there to the ski lodge in Kaybee and we played there, I think, three days. Then we drove from there to Minneapolis where we had about a week. This was right outside Minneapolis called Mendota, called the Jazz Emporium.
We played there two days and then we had a recording, our first recording with this band, in Minneapolis.
That was the first recording that you made with the Legends?
Yes.
It was made where?
In Minneapolis, Minnesota.
Then we left there and went to
Grand Rapids, Michigan where we played two nights.
Is that record obtainable?
Yes, we have it; but not in the stores. He sells it at concerts.
I see. Special mail order?
You could get it that way; yes.
What's the label?
I'll have to think.
All right. Go right on, Mr. Blakeney.

Then from Minneapolis we went to Grand Rapids; from Grand Rapids we went to New York and played a place there called Cami Hall, right across from Carnegie Hall. From New York we went up to Bridgeport, Connecticut. From there to Peterboro, New Hampshire; New Hampshire
to Stowe, Massachusetts.
This was into 1974 then; right? Or was it '73?
This was '73. Putney, Vermont, Hillsboro-- that's in New Hampsire. In Putney, Vermont we played Windom College.
What was the reception like?

Very good. When we first organized the band went over real big--'73, '74, '75, just the Legends. We didn't have no show, just the Legends. Then it began to slow down a little bit, we didn't get too many repeat engagements, and I think in '78 we added on our package, four dancers and a girl singer, which we now have.
That's the set up that you now have.
Right; we call
Who are the dancers?
An old time dancer named--you'll have to excuse me on my memory.
That's quite all right, Mr. Blakeney.

Anyway, it's now 1000 Years of Jazz, from 100 Years of Jazz. A 1000 Years from the Legends of Jazz. We still carry our name, featuring--1000 Years of Jazz, featuring the Legends of Jazz and the original hoofers, they call them. They called it 1000 Years of Jazz because if you add up all the years, it comes somewhere close to a thousand.
Such longevity. We should all be so lucky.
Would you like to reiterate
some of the experiences that you had travelling with this group? You've been to Europe now how many times?
Oh, I don't know, twenty times I guess.
At least twenty times.
Five times in one year.
You went to Europe five times in one year? What year was that?
1978, I think.
Did you just travel all over the continent?
Oh, yes, every western country--every country in western Europe. We played every country in western Europe.
What was that reception like?
Oh, Europe is very good with the Legends; very good.
Did you find any of the people knew exactly who you were?
Yes they did. Barry said that one of the reasons that he wanted me was that the people over there know you, they heard your records and know about you.
That was due to the fact that on one of the oldest records, somebody took it off of the radio and sent it to Europe and made an LP out of it.
We still have a lot of that kind of thing unfortunately, with the illegal taping of records. We're glad you had a good reception there.

Very good. We didn't got to Europe until the next year, February, and this was in September when we made the New England tour and we came back home. In February, we also made a partial tour of the states and

Europe. This is when I almost didn't make, I almost caught a cold and almost didn't make it and Joe Darenbourg didn't make. When he got to London he had a touch of pneumonia and had to be sent back home.
Then there was this boy that looked like a girl--
Who was that?
I showed you a picture there of the band.
Oh, I don't remember who that was.
Anyway, he took Joe's place.
From London we went onto Germany, Belgium, Sweden, Denmark, and came back in March, I think.
Did you meet many of the European musicians?
Oh, yes.
Did they sit in with you?
No, they didn't sit in with us.
They were just so honored to be in your presence I'm sure.
We were playing concerts, you know, so we couldn't have sit-ins.
I understand.
Sometimes we'd go to a party and they'd sit in; once in a while but very seldom because everybody was tired after a concert.

Accommodations weren't so good our first trip over, because Barry had just started out, he didn't have too much money /and so we stayed in the cheapest hotels, but later one we changed that. We all have singles now, nobody doubles anymore. That was '74.
'75 was a good year too, one of our best years, 1975.
But '78 was the year
that you went five times in one year; right? Yes.
We went over there one time just to play one job.
Where was that?
In France.
What was the occasion?
Just a concert.
One concert, all the way to France.
The power of music; the power of jazz.
We got two days pay for it.
And a trip to France.
I don't like to fly anymore.
Well you had quite a bit of it.
A little bit too much of it.
Yes, I'm sure, with the jet lag and coming back home.
And our boss, our boss was in New York--
The agent?
I can't think of it now.
That's quite all right, maybe we can think of it later.

He had something to do with Eastern Airlines, and so he tried to make all our travels on Eastern Airline. Everytime we go to New York from Los Angeles we had to go by way of Atlanta instead of direct.
That was to keep the money in the family.
Since the group of dancers and the girl singer have been added to the Legends, have you played any places down South, and what might be the response?
It's very good
What kinds of people do you find in your audiences down South now, any age group?
All ages.
All ages?
Teens up to in the eighties and nineties, grandmas and great grandmas.
I'm surprised at the youngsters who go for our music. I've seen teenage girls, even black teenage girls, come up to me and say you're so wonderful, I just want to kiss you.
You like that, don't you?
(Laughing)
Of course the audiences now are mixed, even in the South.
Integrated audience, yeah. A far cry from fifty years ago.
I can tell you a little tale about Lionel's band when I
first started with him, when we first went on the road.
Our first job was in Santa Barbara.
This was in California too, not in the south.
This is 1935, my first tour with Lionel.

We got to Santa Barbara early, we had to play two nights there, so we got there in time to go to the jobs. So we didn't look for any place to stay until after we got to work. So we went to work that first night, Gladys was the boss, she was the head of the band, unofficially, and she goes to the big hotel, the Biltmore Hotel, in Santa Barbara.
Anyway, there was a youngster on the desk that night and he didn't care who we were, he said how many are you. He signed us all up and we went to our room and spent the night in bed, except me,

because I had friends in Santa Barbara, so me and my trombone player--we were buddies. The next morning when the boss came in and found out this colored group was in the hotel, he started wringing his hands, 'Oh, what am I going to do; if my regular customers find out they'll all leave; I'll tell you what I'll do, if you all just quietly leave, I won't charge you anything for last night.'
Can you imagine that, in California.
This was 1935 in Santa Barbara, California.
We're not talking behind the Mason-Dixon line.
Not at all. So Gladys talked to Paul Howard--he was kind of the business manager, and they accepted it.
What could they do at that time?
Well, we only spent one night there, it was clean, nice, fine room, a fine bed and everything, for nothing.
So the next night they put us up in a cheap hotel, because we had to stay another night.
That was an incident we had on our first stop on tour with Lionel in 1935, in California.
Not down South.
Now back to the Legends.

I'm glad you brought that out because many people think that bigotry and segregation was only in the South, and many of the "northern" cities and states practiced it also, just a little bit more--at times, discreet. The signs weren't up but you could read the lips and you knew that you were not wanted. So I'm told.
I ran into a lot

of that.
In my career I missed one season tour I made with the Georgia Minstrels, and they were booked by Fanchon Marco; they had more people working for them than any agency in the country at that time.
I heard of it, Mr. Blakeney.
Well we ran into a lot of prejudice on that tour.
What year was that?

1932 to 1933, from August to April of the next year, a whole season. In fact, I quit the tour in Bridgeport, Connecticut, because I got tired of them.
I really enjoyed that tour because we played the largest and the finest theaters in the country.
Who were you with at that time?
The Georgia
Minstrels.
Oh, I see.

But we were booked by Fanchon Marco. Fanchon Marco had groups every week he had a group at a theater for one, the next group we moved to another city and another group would follow us. He had about twenty, twenty-five groups working at the same time, all over the country.
Was it an integrated group?
No, no, it was all black.
A Minstrel band.
Minstrel, all black.

We played San Francisco one week, Oakland one week, with some one-nighters in-between. We played Portland, Oregon one week, Seattle, Washington one week, Vancouver one week, then came back down into Washington and played some one-nighters or two-
nighters until we got to Denver, Colorado. We played all through Idaho, the State of Washington, until we got down to Denver, only Christmas, Colorado. That was/1932.

You know we were talking primarily during this section about the Legends of Jazz. It is evident that from the discrimination and the segregation the musicians had to face during the thirties and even to the forties, did not only exist in the South but in the North as well.
Oh, yes.
I'm sure when you went down South in recent months and years to see the change.
In fact they were nicer down there to us than they were up North.
I've heard that. The hypocrisy of the North was quite unreal.
I know we played a little small town in Arkansas, a date in Arkansas,/ those people were so
nice you just couldn't believe it.

You can't believe that it was once the way it was. It's come a long way. I think it was Martin Luther King who once said that the South would come into its own in terms of social progress much faster than the North, because the North was yet trying to pretend as though it didn't exist. Many of the southern states have come head on with the issue.
Yes, in the South they had one common thing they'd always tell us; 'You all come back.'
Have you ever been into Mississippi with your group, the Legends?
No. We missed that state and it's my home state. I played Louisiana, Alabama, Georgia, Virginia, Arkansas, all them southern states except Mississippi.
As you entered into the eighties with the Legends, prior to your
recent illness, can you tell us of any significant engagements, unusual experiences you've had working with this group during the eighties?
Well, it's pretty hard to say anything outstanding that I can mention, except it's been rough travelling.
It has its wears and tears.
It's not easy. You'd play a concert tonight--
Yes; kind of explain that to us.
--and you're through with the concert at eleven o'clock; everybody's hungry when you get through the concert--
This is when you're doing one-nighters?
That's right. Sometimes you could find a place

to eat and sometimes you can't, but if you do by the time you get to your hotel it's one or two o'clock in the morning. If you have to play someplace tomorrow night, at a distant city, say a thousand miles away, you have to catch a plane. So you've got to get up early enough to catch this plane, sometimes you have to change. That's struggling with your luggage, in and out of cabs, buses, cars, get to the airport, struggle with your luggage; sometimes there's no skycap to help you.
In a smaller airport.
That's right.
Did you have a road manager?
No, we didn't. Yes, we did have a road manager and he'd try to help as much as he could, this young fellow about twenty-five years old.
The dancers were complaining about how tough it was. Sometimes--like

this last trip we were on before I got sick-- we travelled from New York, worked at Detroit--of course I say we had to travel by Eastern Airlines. Now from New York to Detroit is straight across like this; but we had to go by Atlanta, because that's the way Eastern Airlines is.
You mentioned that earlier about your agent booking exclusively on Eastern Airlines.

We got into Detroit that night after changing at Atlanta, about six or seven o'clock. Then we had to get a car. Our first date was a little town 150 miles north of Detroit--I'll get to that later. So we stopped at Lansing, Michigan--that's the capital--spend the night there. So for some reason or another, he decided he would drive his car, 150 miles to Lansing I knew a lot of people in

Lansing from my home town, so I rented a car for myself, get to get around for myself. So that night I had the car and I had to turn it back the next day, I said instead of riding all jammed up with the rest of the guys I'd just drive my own car, and so I did.
They all left me in my hotel room and one of the dancers came up and asked me if I was all right and I said yes. I said I'll see you a little later and they left ahead of me.

So I got in my car and started driving; I had the directions and I found myself getting sleepy, so I stopped. I got a sandwich and two cups of coffee, and I don't drink coffee in the evening. So I started out again and I got lost and I came all the way back, about fifty miles back, to try and find my way straight again.
I finally got myself all straight again and it was getting almost dark now, and
we were due to play at eight o'clock and it was almost six o'clock now.

So I started driving and I was travelling pretty fast I guess and finally I got on a little narrow road and it was snowing, snow was on both sides and I hit a snowbank. I didn't know but when I woke up, some passerby had picked me out of the car.

They said what happened was I swerved this way, back this way and back this way and backed up into the snowbank, against the snowbank and I was asleep, still unconscious. Some passerbys came and pulled me out of the car, and they saw who I was--Oh, you're with the group that's going to play, well, we're on our way to the concert.' I said, 'What happened? Where am I?' They said, 'You're in Mighican.' 'What am I doing in Michigan?' I was out, you see.
Anyway they took me onto the theater. When we got to the theater the
boss was looking for me because it was about five minutes to eight.
I told him about my accident and he said are you ready to go on and I said I'm ready and he said you ain't ready to go on, you're going to the hospital. He would not let me play.

The manager--it was Floyd Turnham's girlfriend, she travelled with him, she took me to the hospital and they examined me from head to toe. I got a bill for it. They said there was nothing seriously wrong, I had a little bleeding on my lungs or something like that. I had a couple bumps on my head, which was a concussion.
Do you think that might have been the result of--
Wait a minute. That's the cause of it.
Anyway the x-ray then didn't show it, but the doctor told me it's liable to show up later.
So we came home after that and I made another tour. This is February 22 when the accident happened. Two weeks later is when I fell out of bed. It was a concussion.

The last week on tour we were in Florida most of the time. North Carolina, Louisiana, we played I think seven concerts in five days. That one week I was so weak the guys had to help me on and off the bandstand. This clot was working, but I didn't realize it, I was just getting weak.

I was so weak that they had to get a wheelchair to put me on the plane. This is in Atlanta, coming to Los Angeles. My wife wasn't going to meet me because I used to catch the bus at the airport and she would meet me at the hotel, but this manager called my wife from Atlanta and he said you better meet your husband, don't let him take no bus because he's not feeling well; so she met me.
She got me home all right and the next day I was supposed to go to the doctor but I didn't go. Tuesday I went to the doctor and my regular doctor sent me over to the Kaiser where the specialist was.
He checked me and examined me but didn't follow up like the doctor told him, the doctor said to check to two knocks on the head and he'll probably discover the blood clot; but he didn't.
So this was Tuesday and I came on home and went to sleep that night and that's the last I remember.
You've had quite a spell.
For the three weeks after the time that I had the accident which caused it all.
These are some of the rigors of the road. Even now when you have to drive.
I told myself I

was going to quit, but it's hard. I told myself three years ago I was going to quit. I get home and I'm only home for two or three weeks and I want to play some more. That's the way it's been all these years. My family wants me to quit; my sisters are mad at me.
We just thank God that He had His hand on your shoulder somewhere and you're back with us again. It was a pretty close call there.
Yes. And I still-- if I ever get my strength back, I will probably go back on the road.
Mrs. Blakeney, did you hear that?
That's quite all right, Mrs. Blakeney, I think he's going to think about it again.
What is he thinking about?
I just said if
I can ever get my full strength back, I'll probably go back on the road.
Oh, dear, my goodness gracious, honey, I don't know about that.
It's in the blood.
All right, if you have to do, I guess you just have to do it.
Every musician should have such a lovely wife.
I was in Sacramento about a month ago at a jazz festival up there and there were tears in my eyes at the reception I got.
I'm sure. You're well loved.
Somebody said, 'There's Andrew Blakeney!'
You've given a lot to music and given a lot to the world, and you're still giving. It's a pleasure to talk

to you. You've given so much and as I said, God's been good to you, you're still with us and we love you, and the world loves you. You've been fortunate, you have a lovely wife and for those of you who will be hearing this interview, I have never sat in a more comfortable home or been made so welcome as I have been in this home while doing this interview. I am honored to be here in your presence, Mr. Blakeney.
Thank you. I feel good having you here and knowing your parents and close your father and I were to each other.
I just saw Lionel this past Father's Day and I know he was close to my father, [he] was his friend too.
Lionel has changed quite a bit. He's a big shot, he's a millionaire.
Yes, he's a very
wealthy man. He spent many years here in Los Angeles though and they gave him a star out here. What is it, the Walk of Fame?

Do you want to tell us anymore-- I guess that's all you could tell us about the Legends because you really went right up through the accident you had and the subsequent illness as a result of it. If you could say anything to the young listeners--
I could say that I didn't like some of the transportation problems that they provided for us.
That is with this last group?
Yes, with the Legends. Sometimes I didn't like the hotel.
As you look back over you life as a professional musician, I'm
sure you have many thoughts. Have you ever, at anytime, thought well, if I had to do it over again I would do it a different way?
I think I'm satisfied with it; I don't think I'd go back and do it any different because the experience I received, it was a wonderful experience. I couldn't have had it any other way.
I'm sure you probably wouldn't have seen as much of the world had it not been for jazz.
I've seen some of the swell spots and stayed at hotels and resort places that people pay thousands of dollars. Not only did we get it free, we got paid for it.
In your experiences with Kid Ory, you mentioned briefly that you did a picture with him called Cross Fire?
That's right.
To digress a bit,
could you elaborate on that for us?

The director told us to play at the opening and there was you know, they didn't use much music; didn't read much; no music involved, and so they had me play something like a cadenza to start off with; Barney Bigard was in that picture.
(Side A of Tape 3 ended at this point.)
(Side B of tape 3 begins at this point.)
Tell us a bit about that movie, and I think there's something significant about it that relates to the blacklist that there was with the Red scare out in Hollywood, some years ago.
The actors in the picture were controversial and so was the story. The story was something pertaining to race also.
I saw the picture in one of the southside theaters and I think I saw it on T.V., a rerun of it.
The personnel of that movie was myself, Kid Ory, Buster Wilson, Montudie Garland, Barney Bigard and Ram Hall.
It was filmed in Hollywood?
In Hollywood. RKO.
Mr. Blakeney, as far as your recording experiences were, what do

you remember as your most--you feel--your most significant performance; when you think you played best? You mentioned that in your earlier life you didn't receive the recognition--that you were playing very well but you did not receive the popular recognition that often happens to musicians. You had a very, very long span when you did no recordings.
Your first recordings were made, I believe, around--well you tell me, with Reb Spikes.
The first recording was around 1925 when I first came to California.
Then you also did some more recording, and I will give a complete discography at the end of this interview, with Sonny Clay in 1925; is that correct?
Yes.
There was a span from 1925 until 1947 where we have no recordings;
perhaps there were some done but we have no record of them. The first was This Is Jazz.
That was done with Kid Ory?
That was done with Kid Ory.
Do you want to tell us something about that record date?
That was done at old KHJ radio station and we had an audience. I didn't know it was going to be recorded, but it was.
You didn't know you were coming for a record date?
No, I didn't know it was going to be a recording; to me it was just a concert.
That's the thing again, recording and the musicians don't even know what's going on.
On that date was Joe Darensbourg--everybody was the same except it wasn't Barney Bigard.
Was that on Circle label?
Yes.
So it was a broadcast at KHJ?
KHJ.
You also did some recordings later on with Kid Ory in 1961.
That was on the Verve label.
As I said before, would you like to comment on any of your records that you made during your lifetime? What you think was your best, did you have any compositions of your own?
My playing, according to my own opinion, was with Kid Ory on Verve.
That was in 1961?
1961. The rest of them weren't actually recordings, somebody took off and made a record of it on their own and later on off a radio broadcast and later on somebody made an LP out of it.

I think that's what prompted the musician's union to outlaw this taping on engagements, because so many musicians had been exploited, particularly black musicians, have been exploited. People would go, oh, I just want to record this, this is for my own pleasure and then some years later you hear it and you see people making money off of it. Many musicians have experienced this, and I think it still goes on to some degree.
Yes it does. I can remember one incident, we were in Bonn, Germany--
Is that recently?
Five or six years

ago.
We were playing at a concert
and the hall was just packed and the movies,
T.V. stations, had all their equipment getting
ready to go up to record everything, and
Barry Martyn flipped. Barry went to talk
with the promoters to get this thing straight,
but he had told them right up front that no
recordings were to be made unless prearrange-
ments were made and the proper--
So you would be paid.
Right.

So he goes upstairs and stayed
there for quite a while. We were sitting
there on the bandstand and these Germans are
getting nervous out there and began making
a lot of noise--
Stomping their feet?

Stomping their
feet.

I sent word up to come down
and play something because these people were

going to do something to us. (laughing) So Barry sent word, never mind, just be still, everything will be all right, but those people were stomping their feet, wanting to know when we were going to play. They paid big money to come see us. So anyway, finally Barry came down with an agreement. They were going to give us a hundred dollars cash that night just for the recording; and then I was at ease. You know the Germans, they're kind of mean--they can be. (Laughing)

When they start stomping their feet, they want to hear some jazz, they want to hear it. They really weren't too concerned about what was going to be recorded. You know it's really not--in this country and other countries--I think it's not really policed the way it should be, because they're still ripping off musicians with the "I just want it for my own personal
use" sort of thing.
That's what they say.

Now they've gotten into videotaping so now they just want that for their own personal use. Musicians will have to fight that and the taping that they see in their friends' record collections that they knew nothing about.

That date with Kid Ory on December 5, 1961, you played "Storyville Blues," "Jellyroll Blues," "Booga Boo," "Do You Know What It Means to Miss New Orleans." Which of those were you featured on? Did they feature you on all of those?
Well, almost every tune we were all on.
Have you done much composing at all?
No, no composing. I did some arranging on the dates in Honolulu.
You feel though that that was some of your best presentations, with Kid Ory?
Yes, with Kid Ory.
That was on Verve records.
I should say that I made some records with C.L. Burt, but I wasn't featured on any.
Do you remember the company; might it have been Leon René's company?
I don't know.
I think he had a company about that time. Anyway, I made about three sides with C.L. .... a big band, three trumpets, four saxes and Jake Porter was on one of these records.
Do you remember the names of any of the songs that you did?
Most of them were
C.L.'s compositions.
His own material?
His own material; yes.
About when was that?
This was '44, '45; right in there.

They probably are not obtainable now, but during that period I think the now late Leon Rene, who wrote When The Swallows Come Back to Capistrano, he and his brother Otis, had a record company, the name of which I don't recall, but they did quite a bit of recording with the black musicians because many of the major labels were not recording them at all.
Do you know anything about Jazz at the Philharmonic, when Norman Granz started out?
Oh, yes, I Dixieland played quite a few/jubilees out there,
Gene Norman?
Norman Granz was now the owner of Pablo Records and so many other ventures.
He worked at the Hollywood Bowl two or three times. What's the name of that way out on, where they used to have the circuses--
On Fairfax?
Yes, in that area, just before you get to Fairfax. Our First Dixieland Jubilee was out there.
Frank Bull?
Frank Bull; that's right.
He used to have all the Dixieland there.
I remember a lot of those things as a child.
He's dead now.
I used to know--here we go again, to the listeners--for the per-
sonal implications, I remember I used to run around in the car with my dad with his drums. I kept up pretty well.
Did you ever hear of Gordon Mitchell; I worked with him quite a bit.
I think I remember hearing that name.
He used to have a lot of Dixieland.
Was that at the Hollywood Legions stadium?
That's right, that's where we used to play quite a bit. We had a lot of gigs in Disneyland.
Disneyland still features a lot of jazz. I think you and my father worked at Disneyland together.
Yes, I did. I substituted for about five weeks one time. I enjoyed that out there.

Tell us a little bit about that. It's very important, the traditional jazz, and in recent months and weeks have been more contemporary jazz at Disneyland. In fact there's been all kinds of jazz at Disneyland. There was even Winston Marsal at Disneyland a couple of weeks ago and some other groups, Spyro Gyro.
The time I was out there, the time I took Michael's place--
Michael Delay, the late?
Yes.
I had my business, I had the club. That's one reason I wasn't interested was because the nights I was there I had to have somebody run my place for me.
Money coming from everywhere (laughing).
I enjoyed it out there--who was out there--myself, your father, Joe Darensboug, Harvey Brooks and a bass

player, I can't remember his name. I don't know. I know they had the recreation of the Hot Five out there, remember, at Disneyland some years ago and they had Louie Armstrong, before his passing, and I think Alton sat in in Baby Dodds place, and Johnny St. Cyr was there and Harvey was sitting in for Louie's wife-- what was her name?
Lucille?

No, not Lucille; the lady that wrote 'Just For A Thrill.' Lil Hardin. Disneyland has done much for jazz in terms of amusement centers. A lot of people pass through that make it right away over to the riverboat, the riverboat that they have out there, which is a recreation of the way the bands used to go up the Mississippi River.
We practically opened up Disneyland.
When was that 1956, '57?
I remember--you mentioned his name--
Alvin McNeil?
That's right. His show was out there with us.
He's an outstanding educator and choral conductor.
I remember how the show started, Alvin McNeil was singing across the water, up in the mountains as if he was singing like he just from Africa, the tom-tom numbers.
It was a fine group. They travelled all over the world too with the traditional jubilee singing that I think originated at (inaud Fiske) University.
You know where I used to join him when he had the choir at Independence Church. He had a fine choir.
He came over here one time to do a number with the church, the Methodist Church over here.
Many of our jazz musicians [started] in the church, many of them have never lost that, never cut the cord. It's been an important part of the lives of many people, the church.

Well, I didn't have a musical family. My father knew vocal music, and he taught me how to read vocal music; / and my aunt, my mother's sister, was a piano teacher; that's the only experience I had from my family. Of course I forgot all of that when I left home and started all over again with the trumpet.

There was a guy out at Warner Brothers that was contracted--the unions could hire musicians to come work in the studios. He called me up at my home and wanted to know if I wanted a job in pictures; I told him yes.
Mr. Blakeney, is this
something you're just recalling as we're going along? Yes, it is.
This is an additional movie or something?
Yes.
Fine.

I told him yes and he said be out at Warner Brothers at such and such a time and day, and I was working with the school board, I was working at Hollywood High, I'll never forget it; that's not far from Warner Brothers, you know. I did a lot of angling to get away from school and make a record, play in the movies. Anyway, I got off to make this audition, because most of them jobs I got in the movies, they had about two or three trumpet players and they picked whoever they wanted.

This particular day I was out at Warner Brothers and there were three trumpet players, myself, Mike Delay and somebody else, and they picked me and they out to the studio told me to go / another day sometime after that. First I had to go to the studio for wardrobe. The picture was Bourbon Street Beat.
This was a series; it wasn't just one movie, a one-shot movie, it was a series, because we were out there for about one day a week for four, five weeks.
Can you give us some insight as to who some of the other musicians might have been?
There were five musicians in this group. Eddie Cole, piano--
Brother of Nat Cole?
Brother of Nat Cole, Nat King Cole. Dave Robinson on bass; Sigmund Galloway, clarinet and sax.
Husband of the late Mahalia.
Husband of the late Mahalia Jackson. Jesse Price--
Did you say Jesse Price earlier?

No. And myself on trumpet. Five of us. Out of the five all are gone now except myself, I'm the only one left. As I said this was a series and we would go out there for the day and tell us to shoot a section and /come back the next week and shoot another section. That picture ran for a long time, because I used to look at them on T.V. in my home. That was before my step-daughter got married.
That was Warner Brothers, you said?
Yes.
Perhaps one of the late night movies might show Bourbon Street Beat.

Well, as we conclude this very special interview with you Mr. Blakeney, and we could just talk for hours and hours and hours and hours and use up all of the tape in Los Angeles County, is there anything that you'd like to say in conclusion, from your beginnings in the State of Mississippi up until this afternoon, June 24, 1982, when you're sitting here looking fit as a fiddle. No one would ever know of your most recent, very serious illness; is there anything you'd like to say to those that will be listening to this interview?

I would say the highlight of my musical career was during the thirties. I was playing up and down Central Avenue. I'd say the highlights would be when we were playing the Lincoln Theater because we were exposed to the whole
town on the stage. That was under the direction of Leon Herniford. I think I mentioned that earlier. I don't know if I mentioned the personnel of that band.
No, you didn't. Would you please do that for us?

The personnel of that band was Harold Brown, pianist, Bud Scott on banjo and guitar, on drums it was-- I can't think of his name--on trombone Lloyd Allen, we used to call him Country, on tenor sax was William France, on alto sax was Edward Barnett and on bass was Reginald Jones, we used to call him Jonesy. The leader and director was a saxophonist and violinist, Leon Herniford. This is the Lincoln Theater.
I call that the highlight of my career because--
1931; right?
From there we went to the
Alabam Nightclub, which was the largest and most popular nightclub on our side of town at that time. So we were exposed there to quite a few people.
You believe that the highlights of all of your musical experience were during the thirties?
Yes, during the thirties. Later in the thirties I went to in Los Angeles the Cotton Club, which was THE job for black musicians in those days.
You mentioned a violinist, and before closing this I want to ask you about another musician, a violinist, do you ever remember Atwell Rose?
Yes I do, very well.
Could you just give us a little bit of information about him, as you recall it?
All I know is he
played with Montudie Garland down at the 111 Dance Hall, for years. Montudie was down there about ten, eleven years.
Did you know anything about his background?
No, I didn't. I know he lived in Los Angeles.
Atwell Rose is his name.
He had a white wife.
You could have any color wife you want, white, black, purple, or pink.
He was about the only one at that time. The first one among us musicians to cross the line.
Yes, the color line; you didn't cross it too much, not openly anyway.
Who was that that once said--I think Adam Clayton Powell, or someone, said
there's been lots of night time integration for many, many years. I guess that was a little unusual in those days.

The last time I saw Atwell Rose was in San Francisco after I got back here from Honolulu. I think he was playing or visiting, and I don't think he lived long after that. I think he used to live on 22nd Street; do you remember the Rosebud Theater?
The Rosebud Theater was on Central Avenue, near Washington.
That's right. Alton and Atwell Rose used to live on 21st or 22nd Street.
I believe he knew my dad quite well.
Oh, yes.
I think that's how I remember the name.
Who was your dad
working with when I first came out here? I think he was working with Charlie Echols.
Was Charlie Echols a dancer?
A trumpet player. His daughter turned out to be an entertainer.

So I recall that the highlight of my playing--of course I held some very important positions as a trumpet player, and one of those important positions was when I played at the Burbank Theater. I was there sixteen months in the pit.
We spoke about that earlier in the interview.

Another time that was very interesting was when I made a cross-country tour with the Georgia Minstrels working for Fanchon Marco; that was another one of the highlights in my career. I enjoyed that, playing to large audiences, and I remember we opened in St. Louis at one of

the largest theaters in the country at that time. I think they had about three large theaters that seated over 5,000 people and one of them was the Fox Theater in St. Louis and another was the Fox Theater in Detroit and I think the other one was the Roxy in New York.
Our first appearance in St. Louis was a matinee and we stood 2,000 people in the aisles, besides the 5,000 seats. That was the Georgia Minstrels.
That was also one of the highlights of your many, many years as a jazz musicians.

And you know, this was during the Depression now and we played to crowded, packed houses everywhere we went. This was 1932-33, right in the middle of the Depression. People were still going to theaters in those days; they didn't have enough money but they'd still go see a
show.
I guess they needed some entertainment, or something to keep them going in view of the very rough' times that they were experiencing economically.

Oftentimes, the musicians and artists find work in a time when it's most difficult for other people, when other people are having very difficult times economically; oftentimes the artists, the musicians and the actors, their work increases somewhat because people need an outlet.
That's a fact.

We might be experiencing some of that right now, with the economic picture as it presently is and the upsurge in the motion picture industry and some of the jazz concerts; people need an outlet from the rigors of unemployment and the more depressing side of life.
I can remember during the Depression, the little jobs I did
have, didn't pay much money but the tips were more than the salaries. It looked like people gave away more money than they do now.

Mr. Blakeney, needless to say, this has been a wonderful experience for me. Perhaps I did say it once, and we could go on and on and on; your memories are so vivid of all of your travels and all of your contacts with all kinds of people, you shared so willingly with me in this interview.
Your contribution to our great American artform, jazz, are immeasureable. I want to thank you for the many, many years you've given a sincere effort to perpetuate this music.
To those of you that will be listening to this interview throughout the years, I certainly hope that you will enjoy listening to it as much as I did enjoy interviewing Mr. Andrew Blakeney.
I would like to proceed with the discography and pertinent information relative to the recording career of Mr. Andrew Blakeney.
Mr. Blakeney's discography is not very extensive. However, he recorded with some of the most important musicians of each era; musicians like Lionel Hampton, Kid Ory, and Ed Garland.
Mr. Blakeney recorded in the early twenties, in the 1940's, the 1960's and '70's.

When questioned about the circumstances surrounding musicians during the recording experiences of the early twenties, Mr. Blakeney states that he was not paid for the dates that he did with Reb Spikes or with the Sanny Clay Orchestra. However, he did receive money in the forties and later on into the sixties and seventies.
He said in the twenties the musicians were just 'excited and happy' to

have their names on a record. The scale during the thirties, he recalls, was approximately $25 to $33 per four side. During the forties period, he did several recordings with the C.L. Burk Orchestra. He was performing at that time at the Club Alabam. Mr. Blakeney did not recall the name of the label. It was possibly a label owned by Leon Rene, a black composer and owner of a record company in the city of Los Angeles at that time.

When questioned about the physical environment of the recording studio in the twenties, Mr. Blakeney stated that it was very, very simple. It had one large room with two mikes and they had a very difficult time trying to balance the sound. He recalls very vividly one of his recording dates in which they had to put Lionel Hampton's drums outside of the recording studio because he was so loud at the time. I think this is also indicated at an earlier
part of our interview.

appeared were entitled, 'I'm Busy and You Can't Come In;' 'Wang Wang Blues;' 'Down in Jungletown;' 'Tuxedo Junction;' 'The World is Waiting for the Sunrise;' 'After You're Gone;' 'I'll Be With You Where You Are.' As we proceeded with the discography of Mr. Andrew Blakeney he was able to recall information relative to his recording experiences that I was not made aware of at an
earlier time. He continues throughout his career to perform with some of the finest musicians available at each stage of his recording career.

Mr. Blakeney recalls that he rehearsed with the Jellyroll Martin Orchestra in Chicago, just two days before coming to California in 1925. This was to have been the first record that was ever recorded by Jellyroll Martin. If he had remained in Chicago he would have been a part of that first record session. However, he was very anxious to get to California and left before doing so. Many of his earlier recordings are now collectors items and as time progresses the others, I am sure, will be in this category.
Mr. Blakeney reiterates sharp contrast in the recording procedures in the very beginning till now. Jazz is an immortal artform and these recordings will help preserve its history.
